subject: physics
title: Thermal Physics Adventure 1: Temperature, heat and specific heat capacity
welcome_lead: Today you'll measure specific heat with q = mcΔT.
meta_desc: Physics — temperature scales, internal energy, specific heat capacity c, q = mcΔT.
final_note: You learned T(K) = T(°C) + 273; absolute zero = 0 K; specific heat capacity c specifies how much energy raises 1 kg by 1 K.

concepts.def: Total random KE + PE of particles
J/kg/K to raise 1 kg by 1 K

walkthroughs.body_html:
Celsius: water freezes 0°C, boils 100°C at 1 atm.

Kelvin (absolute): 0 K = -273.15°C. T(K) = T(°C) + 273.15.

Increments equal: ΔT in K = ΔT in °C. Always use K in gas laws + Boltzmann.

Internal energy U = total random KE + PE of particles in a system.

For an ideal gas, no PE between particles → U depends only on T.

For real solids/liquids, U includes vibrational + bond energies.

q = m c ΔT

Water: c = 4180 J/kg/K (extremely high — why oceans moderate climate).
Copper: c = 385 J/kg/K.
Aluminium: c = 900 J/kg/K.

Lab: drop hot metal into cooler water; m_metal c_metal (T_metal - T_final) = m_water c_water (T_final - T_water).

mcqs.q: If c for water is 4180 J/kg/K, energy to heat 2 kg by 10 K:
What property of a sound wave determines its pitch?
options: The frequency — higher frequency means higher pitch.
Amplitude determines pitch — a bigger wave is a higher-pitched note.
The speed of the wave determines pitch — faster waves sound higher.
The water turns into wave material and changes state.

mcqs.q: When a wave travels through water, what happens to the water itself?
options: The water turns into wave material and changes state.
The water oscillates about a fixed point; the wave transfers energy, not matter.
The water moves along with the wave from one place to another.
The speed of the wave determines pitch — faster waves sound higher.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between nuclear fission and fusion?
options: The speed of the wave determines pitch — faster waves sound higher.
Fission and fusion are the same process, just at different scales.
Fission splits a heavy nucleus into smaller ones; fusion joins light nuclei into a heavier one.
Fission combines small atoms into bigger ones, and fusion splits them.
